concepts.name: Mughal Revenue System and its Impact on Trade: Zabt, Dahsala, and Nasaq
key_dimensions: Distinction between Zabt (measurement-based), Nasaq (estimated), and Batai (crop-sharing) systems and their regional applicability
Todar Mal's Dahsala (Ten-Year Settlement) — its mechanism, geographic scope, and limitations (not universal across empire)
How revenue extraction affected the surplus available for trade and merchant capital formation
UPSC trap: Dahsala was NOT applied to all provinces — Bengal, Sindh, Kashmir used different systems

concepts.name: Karkhanas: Imperial Workshops as Economic Institutions
key_dimensions: Dual function: production for imperial consumption AND as a mechanism of state control over skilled artisans
Relationship between karkhanas and the broader market economy — whether they suppressed or stimulated commercial craft production
Abul Fazl's description in Ain-i-Akbari vs. actual economic role debated by historians (Irfan Habib vs. others)
UPSC trap: Karkhanas were NOT factories in the modern sense — workers were not wage laborers in a capitalist framework

concepts.name: Mughal Monetary System: Currency, Coinage, and Market Integration
key_dimensions: Tri-metallic currency system — gold (mohur), silver (rupiya), copper (dam) and their exchange ratios
Sher Shah's currency reform as the foundation — Akbar's continuation and standardization
Role of sarrafs (money changers/bankers) in currency exchange and credit facilitation
UPSC trap: The rupiya introduced by Sher Shah Sur, NOT by Akbar — Akbar standardized and expanded it

concepts.name: Inland Trade Routes and Infrastructure: Sarais, Roads, and River Networks
key_dimensions: Grand Trunk Road (Sadak-i-Azam) — its role in military logistics vs. commercial trade facilitation
Network of sarais (rest houses) — spacing, administration, and their role as nodes of commercial exchange
River-based trade: Ganga-Yamuna system, Bengal waterways — comparative advantage over road transport
UPSC trap: Sarais served multiple functions (postal, military, commercial) — questions may isolate one function

concepts.name: Mughal Port Towns and Maritime Trade: Surat, Hugli, and Masulipatnam
key_dimensions: Surat as the premier port — its administration under a Mutasaddi, role as 'Gateway to Mecca' (hajj trade)
Comparative analysis: Surat (west coast) vs. Masulipatnam (east coast, Golconda overlap) vs. Hugli (Bengal)
Mughal state's ambivalent maritime policy — lack of a navy and dependence on Portuguese cartazes
UPSC trap: Mughal Empire had NO significant naval power — maritime security was NOT a Mughal priority unlike land empire

concepts.name: The Dastak System and European Trading Companies
key_dimensions: Dastak as a pass/permit system — its original purpose and how European companies (especially English) abused it
Role of the dastak in triggering the conflict leading to the Battle of Plassey (Siraj ud-Daulah vs. English)
Distinction between farman (imperial grant) and dastak (trading permit) — hierarchical relationship
UPSC trap: The 1717 Farman of Farrukhsiyar granted to English EIC is often confused with dastak privileges

concepts.name: Banjaras and Itinerant Traders: The Backbone of Internal Commerce
key_dimensions: Banjaras as specialized long-distance grain and commodity carriers — their organization in tanḍas
Their critical role in supplying Mughal armies — military-commercial nexus
Relationship between Banjara networks and market towns (qasbas and mandis)
UPSC trap: Banjaras are often overlooked in favor of merchant guilds — their role was MORE significant for bulk commodity movement

concepts.name: Merchant Communities and Trading Networks: Multanis, Marwaris, and Gujarati Merchants
key_dimensions: Multani merchants in Central Asian trade vs. Gujarati merchants in maritime/Indian Ocean trade — geographic specialization
Marwari (Mahajan) networks — hundis, credit instruments, and their role in integrating distant markets
Caste and community as organizing principles of Mughal commerce — vs. state-organized trade
UPSC trap: Mughal trade was largely in PRIVATE hands, NOT state-monopolized — contrast with mercantilist European states

concepts.name: Hundi System and Indigenous Banking: Pre-Modern Credit Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Hundi as a bill of exchange — its types (Darshani, Muddati) and their functions in long-distance trade
Sarrafs vs. Mahajans vs. Seths — overlapping but distinct roles in Mughal credit economy
How the hundi system reduced transaction costs and enabled market integration across the subcontinent
UPSC trap: The hundi system is indigenous — it predates and is DISTINCT from European bills of exchange, though functionally similar

concepts.name: Mughal Taxation on Trade: Rahdari, Zakat, and Internal Tolls
key_dimensions: Rahdari (transit duty) as the primary tax on moving goods — its rates, collection points, and evasion methods
Akbar's abolition of internal tolls in 1564 — its economic significance and whether it was fully implemented
Zakat on Muslim merchants — its theoretical vs. actual application in Mughal fiscal system
UPSC trap: Akbar abolished some internal tolls but rahdari was NOT completely eliminated — partial reform, not total free trade

concepts.name: Mughal India's Export Commodities and Trade Balance
key_dimensions: Key exports: textiles (cotton, silk), indigo, saltpeter, spices — their relative importance and production regions
The bullion import phenomenon — why Mughal India was a 'sink' for New World silver
Indigo trade: Bayana and Sarkhej as production centers — role of European demand in stimulating Indian agriculture
UPSC trap: India had a FAVORABLE trade balance (surplus) in the Mughal period — it exported more than it imported in value terms

concepts.name: Mughal Central Asian Trade: The Overland Silk Route Connection
key_dimensions: Kabul as the entrepôt — trade with Persia, Central Asia, and China through the overland route
Commodities exchanged: horses, dried fruits, and Central Asian goods vs. Indian textiles and spices
Decline of overland trade due to Safavid-Uzbek conflicts and rise of maritime routes — impact on Mughal economy
UPSC trap: Mughals were DEPENDENT on Central Asia for war horses — this was a strategic vulnerability, not just a trade fact

concepts.name: Role of Qasba and Mandi in Mughal Commercial Network
key_dimensions: Qasba as a market town — its position between village and city in the commercial hierarchy
Mandi as a specialized commodity market — its role in agricultural surplus commercialization
How the expansion of qasbas reflects increasing monetization of the Mughal economy (Irfan Habib's thesis)
UPSC trap: Not all qasbas were purely commercial — many were administrative centers with commercial functions as secondary

concepts.name: Portuguese Estado da India and its Impact on Mughal Trade
key_dimensions: Cartaz system — Portuguese licensing of Indian Ocean trade and its impact on Mughal maritime commerce
Mughal-Portuguese relationship: pragmatic accommodation despite religious conflict (hajj ships, trade concessions)
Portuguese control of Hormuz and Goa — chokepoints that affected Mughal access to Persian Gulf and Red Sea trade
UPSC trap: Mughals were NOT completely subservient to Portuguese — they had leverage through controlling Surat and hajj routes

concepts.name: Artisan Classes and the Putting-Out System in Mughal Textile Trade
key_dimensions: The relationship between merchant capital and artisan production — advances (dadni system) binding weavers to merchants
Dadni merchants and their role as intermediaries between European companies and Indian weavers
Question of proto-industrialization in Mughal India — why it did NOT transition to industrial capitalism (Irfan Habib's 'Crisis of the Indian Economy')
UPSC trap: Artisans were NOT free market agents — the dadni/advance system created dependency, often exploitative

concepts.name: Mughal State's Role in Trade: Regulation, Facilitation, and Revenue Extraction
key_dimensions: Balance between revenue extraction (rahdari, customs) and trade facilitation (road/sarai infrastructure)
Absence of a mercantilist trade policy — Mughal state did NOT protect domestic industry or promote exports ideologically
Role of the Mir Bahri (port officer) and Mutasaddi in regulating coastal trade
UPSC trap: Mughal approach was REVENUE-MAXIMIZING not development-oriented — fundamental difference from modern state trade policy

concepts.name: Bengal's Commercial Economy: Silk, Cotton, and the Ganga Delta Trade
key_dimensions: Bengal as the richest Mughal subah — its unique commercial economy based on textiles (muslin of Dhaka) and rice surplus
Hugli as a cosmopolitan port — presence of Portuguese, Dutch, English, and Armenian merchants simultaneously
Role of the Jagannath temple network and Bengali merchants in connecting Bay of Bengal trade
UPSC trap: Bengal's wealth made it a TARGET for later Maratha raids (Bargis) and European competition — economic prosperity had political consequences

concepts.name: Armenian and Other Diaspora Merchants in Mughal Trade
key_dimensions: Armenian merchants as key intermediaries in Indo-Persian and Indo-European trade networks
Their legal status under Mughal law — firmans granting special commercial privileges
Comparison with Banias, Multanis, and European companies — what made Armenian networks distinctive
UPSC trap: Armenian merchants were NOT Europeans — they were a distinct trading diaspora often confused with European traders in MCQ options

concepts.name: Decline of Mughal Trade in the 18th Century: Structural and Political Causes
key_dimensions: Nadir Shah's invasion (1739) and its destruction of the monetary economy of Delhi — immediate shock
Structural factors: Maratha disruption of trade routes, jagirdari crisis reducing surplus for commerce
Rise of regional successor states and their impact — both disruptive AND sometimes locally stimulating to trade
UPSC trap: Decline was NOT solely due to European companies — INTERNAL political fragmentation was equally if not MORE significant
